p.x:
I'm twelve years old now. Next year, I'll go to a new school. I can't wait!
When I grow up, I want to be a vet. That's my dream job because I love animals. Maybe I'll have my own animal hospital one day.
I often imagine my life in twenty years. I'll live in a small house with a big garden and lots of pets. My mum says, "Anything is possible if you work hard." Tomorrow, I'll start reading a book about animals. I want to learn as much as I can.

What will life be like in 2050? Nobody can predict the future exactly, but experts have some ideas.
Transport will probably change a lot. Driverless cars may be common, and drone delivery could bring parcels to our windows. Space travel will be cheaper, and some people believe there will even be a colony on Mars. But time travel is still impossible, perhaps forever!
Schools may look very different. Students might use virtual reality to visit ancient Rome or swim with whales. A teacher could appear in class as a hologram. Many people will need to retrain several times in their lives, because new jobs will appear and old ones will disappear.
Not everyone agrees about the future. An optimist believes technology will solve our biggest problems. A pessimist worries about climate change and job losses. The truth is that the future is uncertain, so it's important to plan ahead. In some countries, people still visit a fortune teller to ask about their future, but scientists prefer to make a prediction based on data. What do you look forward to most? It's likely that the world in 2050 will surprise us all.

Throughout history, writers and scientists have tried to imagine the future. Some have described a utopia, a perfect society free from poverty and conflict, while others have warned of a dystopia in which technology is used to control people. The reality will almost certainly lie somewhere in between.
By 2050, nearly seven in ten people are expected to live in cities, and many will live in a megacity of more than ten million inhabitants. Feeding these populations will require new approaches. A vertical farm, in which crops are grown in stacked layers inside buildings, uses far less land and water than traditional agriculture, while lab-grown meat, produced from animal cells without raising livestock, could reduce greenhouse gas emissions dramatically.
Energy is another area of rapid change. Scientists have made important progress towards nuclear fusion, the process that powers the sun, which could one day provide almost unlimited clean energy. Meanwhile, cutting-edge medical technology is advancing quickly: a brain implant has already allowed some paralysed patients to control computers with their thoughts.
The world of work will also be transformed. As automation spreads, some economists argue that governments should introduce a universal basic income, a regular payment to every citizen regardless of employment. Whatever happens, lifelong learning will be essential. Workers will need to upskill continuously to keep pace with technological change, and education will no longer end when people leave school or university.
